prize_parts.citation: for their analyses of nominal rigidities, staggered price and wage setting and monetary policy rules, which established the New Keynesian framework for monetary policy

statement.case_for: B014 remains my first choice. Nominal rigidities, the micro-founded New Keynesian framework and the rule-based view of monetary policy are the working basis of modern central-bank analysis, and the influence on both theory and practice has lasted for decades. The work is fully mature and has been tested through the financial crisis, the zero lower bound and the post-pandemic inflation. The credited contributions are also conceptually distinct. Calvo supplied the tractable pricing friction (time-dependent price setting). Taylor supplied staggered contracts and the policy rule. Woodford supplied the integrated, welfare-based theory of interest and prices. After listening to colleagues I am moving from Woodford, Gali and Taylor to Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. The ballot item is defined by nominal rigidities, and Calvo's pricing device is the primitive on which the New Keynesian Phillips curve rests. Gali's work is very important, but it is largely development, integration and empirical implementation of that structure. It is also co-authored with Gertler and others, so it is harder to isolate as a single originating contribution.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the main weakness. At least six or seven strong claimants (Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gertler, Smets and others) are left out by the three-person cap, and the medium-scale estimated DSGE contribution of Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans would go uncredited. Calvo's contribution is a compact modelling device, and one can ask whether it is a discovery in the sense the Committee normally rewards. The framework's record in 2008 and in the 2021-23 inflation is debated, and heterogeneous-agent models may be seen as its successor. Monetary and macro policy work has also been recognised repeatedly (Lucas, Sargent and Sims, Kydland and Prescott, Bernanke), so the area may look saturated.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B014 first and argues that Calvo (price setting), Taylor (contracts and rule) and Woodford (synthesis and normative theory) are the most distinct conceptual contributions, while accepting that excluding Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets is a real cost.
responses.response: This argument moved me on one name. I replaced Gali with Calvo because the prize case is built on nominal rigidities, and Calvo's pricing friction is the origin of the microfounded Phillips curve. Gali's work is largely a development of that structure. I do not think the cost of exclusion is small, though. The estimation and identification contribution of Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans and of Smets and Wouters is what made the framework usable in central banks, and a citation limited to pricing, rules and synthesis leaves that out. I would want the citation worded so that it does not claim to cover the estimated DSGE tradition.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B047 first for its clean Melitz attribution and two decades of confirmation. He ranks B014 second, but notes the tension with the framework's failure to anticipate 2008 and the 2021-22 inflation, and the apparent saturation of monetary macro.
responses.response: I agree that B047 has the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, and that counts for it. I do not accept the forecasting-failure argument as strongly against B014. The Committee rewards originality and lasting influence on how a field analyses its questions, not predictive success in particular episodes. The framework has also been revised after both episodes rather than abandoned. My reasons for ranking B047 below B014 are different. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum have strong claims on the empirical and quantitative side and are not on the credited list, and Krugman's 2008 prize leaves some overlap in subject. Neither is decisive, so B047 stays a serious candidate for me.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B003 first. He sees a clean Kiyotaki and Moore pair, leaves out Gertler and Gilchrist because the financial-accelerator line overlaps the 2022 prize, and judges the timing ripe.
responses.response: I accept the narrower pair, and I now think my opening trio with Gertler was a mistake. Gertler is also on B014, which blurs the credit across the two entries. I partly disagree on the 2022 overlap. Kiyotaki and Moore's collateral-driven amplification is a different mechanism from bank runs (Diamond and Dybvig) and from the Depression-era credit-channel work cited for Bernanke. The overlap is therefore less serious than it first appears. I would still want the Committee to examine it carefully, and I keep B003 as my first alternative because its attribution is cleaner than B014's.

uncertainties: Whether Calvo is the right third name rather than Gali, and whether a citation can avoid implicitly ranking the excluded estimated-DSGE contributors (Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets) below the three named.

Whether the Committee regards monetary and New Keynesian macro as already well covered by earlier prizes, or sees the post-2021 inflation debate and heterogeneous-agent extensions as undermining the representative-agent core.
Whether B003 (Kiyotaki and Moore) should be treated as a distinct achievement from B014 given Gertler's presence on both lists. A two-part configuration is limited by the three-person cap.

For B018, the Committee must decide whether the data-construction contribution outweighs the contested wealth measurement and the r > g interpretation. I cannot verify these methodological disputes from the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for Calvo, Taylor or Woodford. My listed co-authors are in the Uppsala and IFAU labour-economics network and none is on the preferred part. The profile records an institutional overlap with the IIES macro group (Hassler, Krusell) at Stockholm University in 2010-17. That is not a co-authorship, and those two are committee colleagues, not candidates.
